subcomponents.title: Uses scene-kit APIs without bypassing or duplicating them

criteria.rationale: The demo consumes the kit through its public barrel and does not re-implement kit mechanisms. Talk.tsx renders the kit's Presentation with the shared STEPS, a title and an initialMode. The shared EvolvingScene builds the diagram from kit primitives (Appear, Box, Arrow, Frame, Label) and uses the kit's EASE, ENTER_T, ENTER_DELAY, HOOK and hookAttrs. Each step module types itself as the kit's Step and supplies groupKey, scene and payload. Stage owns layer keying, LayoutGroup and AnimatePresence, so the demo has no mount or layout logic of its own. One chip (the question) is a raw motion.div inside the demo's own AnimatePresence. It reuses the kit's HOOK, hookAttrs and timing constants for its data attributes, enter transition and ease, and it needs no layoutId. I do not count that as bypassing the kit.

Scene.tsx imports Appear, Arrow, Box, Frame, Label, EASE, ENTER_DELAY, ENTER_T, HOOK, hookAttrs and SceneProps from '../../presentation-kit'. EvolvingScene composes them and passes `id={ENTIT…
All nine step modules (01 through 09) are `Step<TalkPayload>` with `scene: EvolvingScene`, `groupKey: 'evolving-scene'` and `payload: { stage: N }`.
Stage.tsx: layerKey() and `<LayoutGroup><AnimatePresence><SceneLayer key=...><Scene payload=.../>` are kit-owned.
judging basis: consensus-pass

subcomponents.title: Uses stable identities and appropriate grouped-scene architecture

criteria.rationale: Grouping: all nine steps set groupKey 'evolving-scene' and scene EvolvingScene. Stage.layerKey() returns `group:${groupKey}:${sceneId(scene)}`, so every step maps to the same SceneLayer key. Navigating between steps therefore keeps the existing mounted instance and only changes the payload. A single shared groupKey is correct for this one evolving scene. Identity: entities.ts defines presentation-owned, namespaced ENTITY ids. EvolvingScene passes them as `id` to Box, Frame and Label. Those primitives forward `id` to `layoutId` and to the data-presentation-id hook through nodeAttrs. Arrow takes the same `id` for its node attribute and animates its endpoints in place. The question chip uses ENTITY.question as its key and node-id hook. Newcomers are wrapped in Appear, and the persisting entities stay mounted across stages, so they morph in place. Every ENTITY member is consumed in Scene.tsx: you, prompt, question, skill, ask, answer, tray, card1 to card3, link1, link2, ghost, depth, kit, plug, verify, chain, modify, reveal and revealLabel.
evidence: Steps 01 through 09 each have groupKey 'evolving-scene', scene: EvolvingScene and payload.stage 1 through 9.
steps/index.ts lists step1 through step9 in order.
Stage.tsx layerKey(): `group:${step.groupKey}:${sceneId(step.scene)}` is used as the SceneLayer key inside LayoutGroup and AnimatePresence.
Box.tsx, Frame.tsx and Label.tsx set `layoutId={id}`. Arrow.tsx animates line endpoints with `animate={{x1,y1,x2,y2}}`. shared.ts nodeAttrs forwards the id to HOOK.nodeId.
entities.ts ENTITY members are all referenced as `id={ENTITY.x}` in Scene.tsx, and ENTITY.question is used as a key and a hook value.

subcomponents.title: Entity transitions and persistent grouped scenes

criteria.rationale: Kit primitives are motion elements with a layoutId taken from the stable entity id and a layout transition (LAYOUT_T, EASE). A same-id entity in consecutive steps therefore animates layout in place. Arrow animates its endpoints.
evidence: Box, Frame, Label and SymbolChip set layoutId={id} and transition={{layout:{duration:LAYOUT_T, ease:EASE}}}.
Emphasis uses layoutId with layout="position".
Arrow animates x1,y1,x2,y2 with LAYOUT_T.
judging basis: consensus-pass

criteria.rationale: The requirement is not met for the kit's Arrow entity primitive. When two consecutive steps are ungrouped, Stage gives each one its own SceneLayer key (`step:${id}`). AnimatePresence runs in sync mode inside a LayoutGroup, so the outgoing layer and the incoming layer are mounted together and each one fades its opacity. Box, Frame, Label, SymbolChip and Emphasis pass `layoutId={id}`, so shared-layout projection can carry them between the two layers. Arrow does not: it uses `id` only for the DOM data hook (nodeAttrs) and has no layoutId. Its endpoint animation is local to one instance (`initial={false}`, `animate={{x1,y1,x2,y2}}`). So when an Arrow with the same id is in both ungrouped steps, the incoming instance mounts already at its new endpoints and fades in with its layer, while the old instance fades out at the old endpoints. The entity disappears in one place and reappears in another; it does not animate from its old state to its new state in place. That is the failure the guidance names. Shared.ts and Arrow's own doc comment promise that same-id entities 'morph in place via layoutId' and 'Endpoints animate in place when the same id continues into the next step', but across separate layers nothing implements this. I rule judge A's verdict. Judges B and C are right about the containers: the layers are mounted together and taken out of layout flow, and the layoutId primitives have no initial opacity or delay. But both checked only the layoutId primitives (Box, Label, Frame, SymbolChip) and never considered Arrow. Arrow has no layoutId, so the LayoutGroup projection they rely on does not reach it. Judge C cites the 'cross-fades into a non-grouped step' test, but it only waits for `diagram-box` to exist. It never checks that a persisting entity morphs, so it does not show that the requirement is met.

Arrow.tsx:18-44 has no layoutId. id goes only to nodeAttrs('arrow', id, data). The motion.line uses initial={false} and animate={{x1,y1,x2,y2}}, which interpolates only within one mounted ins…
Arrow.tsx:13-17 doc comment and shared.ts:14 claim same-id entities morph in place, but no cross-layer mechanism exists for Arrow.

Each starts `npm run verify` or the inspect helper with spawnSync, which blocks until that process has exited. Each then asserts only on the exit status, the output, the files written and the manifest. So no test asserts on browser state that is still changing, and none of the full test files quoted contains setTimeout, waitForTimeout, a sleep or a delay call. The only async helper they use, isPortOpen in tests/helpers.ts, is a direct TCP connection probe that resolves on connect or error. It asserts synchronously after act()-wrapped key presses and fireEvent calls. Its one async check uses Testing Library's polling `waitFor`, and it has no timers. When the inspect helper used by the integration test reaches each step, it polls the step index with page.waitForFunction until data-step-index matches the target index. It then waits for a MutationObserver-based settle clock with a polling waitForFunction, not a fixed sleep. Judge A's pass and Judge B's pass match this material. checks.rationale: The dissent votes pass, but its reasoning covers only the layoutId primitives: Box and Label. It does not answer the decider's stated reason, which concerns the kit's Arrow entity primitive. The cited source confirms the decider's reason. In Stage, two ungrouped steps get separate SceneLayer keys (`step:${step.id}`), so each step has its own layer. Arrow has no layoutId. It uses `id` only in nodeAttrs, which sets a data hook. Its only endpoint motion is a `motion.line` with `initial={false}` and `animate={{ x1, y1, x2, y2 }}`, and that animation runs inside a single component instance. So when a same-id Arrow appears in two consecutive ungrouped steps, the incoming copy mounts already at its new endpoints in the new layer, and that layer fades in from opacity 0. Meanwhile the outgoing copy fades out at its old endpoints with the old layer. The entity disappears from one place and reappears in another; it does not animate from its old state to its new state in place. That leaves the requirement unmet for this primitive. Judge C cites the 'cross-fades into a non-grouped step' test, but it only waits for `diagram-box` to exist. It never checks that a persisting entity morphs, so it does not show that the requirement is met.

The inspect helper these tests drive polls the step index with `waitForFunction` and waits on a MutationObserver settle clock. The verification script's own settle delay belongs to the verification-tooling criteria. The review guidance also lists longer fixed settle delays as validator noise. It also follows a polling waitForStepIndex, so it is an extra settle delay after a state wait, not a sleep standing in for one. The criterion concerns how the browser tests wait before asserting. scene-kit.rationale: Mode toggling changes only mode and preserves the current index.

scene-kit.rationale: All specified keys map to the required single-step navigation.
evidence: ArrowRight, Space, and PageDown map to next; ArrowLeft and PageUp map to prev. The hook changes the index by exactly one before clamping.
Parameterized hook tests exercise every required key and verify the resulting index.

scene-kit.rationale: Horizontal touch displacement invokes one-step navigation in the required directions.
evidence: Presentation spreads the hook's touch handlers onto its root. The handlers compare starting and ending clientX positions.
swipeAction maps negative displacement beyond 48 pixels to next and positive displacement to prev; dispatch invokes the same single-step callbacks. The component test exercises both directions.

scene-kit.rationale: Both navigation surfaces directly select their required target index.
evidence: Progress buttons invoke onGoTo(position); Toc buttons invoke onGoTo(start.firstIndex), derived from eraStarts.

scene-kit.rationale: Progress and contents controls expose semantic current state and stable styling hooks.
evidence: Both surfaces emit aria-current='step' for the active item and data-presentation-active='true' or 'false'.

scene-kit.rationale: The keyboard handler leaves navigation keys to the delivered interactive controls.
evidence: isInteractiveTarget recognizes button, a[href], and native form controls through closest(), covering the sample's chrome controls and attribution link.

scene-kit.rationale: Backward navigation at the first step remains at zero.
evidence: prev applies clampIndex(current.index - 1, count), and clampIndex has a lower bound of zero.
The hook boundary test calls prev at initialization and asserts index 0.

scene-kit.rationale: Forward navigation at the last step remains at the last index.
evidence: next applies clampIndex(current.index + 1, count), whose upper bound is count - 1.

scene-kit.rationale: The resize mechanism applies one fit factor to the fixed canvas and fits all four required viewport/mode combinations.

It restricts edits to that presentation's folder and its registry title if necessary, prohibits rerunning the full create flow, and prohibits touching other presentations.

presentation-skill.rationale: The completion gate explicitly requires build, render, and browser composition checks with all required step selections and conditional narrow-viewport inspection.
evidence: Self-verify requires build, verify, and inspection before reporting done.
It directs opening the first, last, and densest or most important steps, and checking the same steps using --narrow for responsive-sensitive presentations.
The procedure finishes with verify and requires its last line to start with PASS; modifications invoke the same gate.

presentation-skill.rationale: The instructions require fixing failures and rerunning checks, and prohibit reporting success while failures remain.
evidence: “Never report success on output that fails. Fix the failure, then re-run the check.”
Visual findings must be addressed and inspection rerun after changes.
The repair loop requires rerunning the failed check and verify; after unsuccessful attempts it requires reporting the error without claiming success.

verification-tooling.rationale: Readiness comes from HTTP probing of the port (probe(url)). The only ownership check is the child's exitCode/signalCode sampled at the top of each loop iteration, before the probe. Readiness is not taken from the child's own announcement, and the child's exit is not raced against readiness. The port is also closed after freePort() before the child binds, so a stale or other server could answer the probe before the child's exit is observed. Guidance names this pattern as a fail, and --strictPort alone is insufficient.
evidence: scripts/verify.mjs waitForPreview(): checks child.exitCode/signalCode, then `if (await probe(url)) return`, then delay(250)
scripts/verify.mjs startPreview(): stdout is captured only for failure output, never parsed for a ready announcement
scripts/verify.mjs freePort(): server.close() before the port is resolved and handed to the child

engineering-quality.rationale: All four script copies spawn the Vite CLI directly through process.execPath in a detached process group. stopPreview sends SIGTERM to the group, escalates to SIGKILL after 5s, and awaits the child's 'exit'. cleanup() runs in run()'s finally block, so success, a thrown failure and an error after the preview started all pass through it. SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers also call it. In both scripts the browser is launched before the preview starts, so a launch failure leaves no preview running. No npm or npx wrapper is killed in place of the server.

The bootstrap template copies of both scripts contain the same stopPreview, cleanup and finally structure

votes.rationale: The verifier does reserve an ephemeral port with freePort() and starts the preview with --strictPort. But readiness comes from HTTP probing of that port, not from the child's own announcement. The only ownership check is the child's exit status sampled at the top of each loop iteration, before each probe. A stale server on that port could answer the first probe before the child's exit is observed. This is the pattern the review guidance names as a fail. A strict port alone does not count, and the child's exit is not raced against readiness.

votes.rationale: Step advance is checked with waitForStepIndex, which compares the data-step-index attribute string to String(expected) within a timeout. If it does not arrive, VerifyFailure('transition', ... stepLabel(index,count) ...) is thrown. Absent or non-numeric data-step-count is not treated as progress: Number(null) is 0 and Number('abc') is NaN, so `!Number.isInteger(count) || count < 1` throws VerifyFailure('render'), which also covers the unreadable-count case. first_results.rationale: The requirement is not met for the kit's Arrow entity primitive. When two consecutive steps are ungrouped, Stage gives each one its own SceneLayer key (`step:${id}`). AnimatePresence runs in sync mode inside a LayoutGroup, so the outgoing layer and the incoming layer are mounted together and each one fades its opacity. Box, Frame, Label, SymbolChip and Emphasis pass `layoutId={id}`, so shared-layout projection can carry them between the two layers. Arrow does not: it uses `id` only for the DOM data hook (nodeAttrs) and has no layoutId. Its endpoint animation is local to one instance (`initial={false}`, `animate={{x1,y1,x2,y2}}`). So when an Arrow with the same id is in both ungrouped steps, the incoming instance mounts already at its new endpoints and fades in with its layer, while the old instance fades out at the old endpoints. The entity disappears in one place and reappears in another; it does not animate from its old state to its new state in place. That is the failure the guidance names. Shared.ts and Arrow's own doc comment promise that same-id entities 'morph in place via layoutId' and 'Endpoints animate in place when the same id continues into the next step', but across separate layers nothing implements this. I rule judge A's verdict. Judges B and C are right about the containers: the layers are mounted together and taken out of layout flow, and the layoutId primitives have no initial opacity or delay. But both checked only the layoutId primitives (Box, Label, Frame, SymbolChip) and never considered Arrow. Arrow has no layoutId, so the LayoutGroup projection they rely on does not reach it. Judge C cites the 'cross-fades into a non-grouped step' test, but it only waits for `diagram-box` to exist. It never checks that a persisting entity morphs, so it does not show that the requirement is met.

audit_results.rationale: The guidance asks two things. First, for two consecutive steps that do not share a scene group, does the step transition keep both steps' entities present together? Second, does the persisting entity stay visible while it moves from its old state to its new state in place, or does it vanish and reappear? The quoted material shows the Arrow primitive fails the second clause. Why the Arrow fails: - Stage.tsx:30-34 gives an ungrouped step its own layer key, `step:${step.id}`. As a result, AnimatePresence (Stage.tsx:73-78) mounts a new SceneLayer for the incoming step and exits the old one. - SceneLayer.tsx:17-21 fades the incoming layer in from opacity 0 and fades the outgoing layer out. - Box.tsx:20 passes `layoutId={id}`, so the LayoutGroup's shared-layout projection can carry a Box across the two layers. Arrow.tsx:21-28 has no layoutId: it uses `id` only in nodeAttrs, which shared.ts:32-37 shows just emits data hooks. - The endpoint animation in Arrow.tsx:35-41 belongs to a single motion.line instance. Because of `initial={false}`, a newly mounted instance starts at its new endpoints. So when an Arrow with the same id appears in both ungrouped steps, the outgoing copy fades out at the old endpoints. The incoming copy fades in, inside its new layer, at the new endpoints. The arrow disappears and reappears instead of animating in place, which is the failure the guidance names. The guidance tells the reviewer to judge the kit's own entity primitives in this ungrouped-step scenario, so this is not a hypothetical-input failure. The doc comments in shared.ts:14 and Arrow.tsx:15-16 promise in-place animation, but the quoted code does not implement it across separate layers. The quoted non-grouped test (Presentation.test.tsx:86-91) only checks that `diagram-box` exists. It does not check that anything morphs, so it does not show the requirement is met.

first_results.rationale: The requirement is met: when the reference sample is missing, verification exits non-zero and the output names the sample phase. In scripts/verify.mjs, checkRegistry() runs after the build and before any browser or preview work. If the reference slug is not registered in src/presentations/index.ts, it throws VerifyFailure('sample registration', ...). In renderPresentation, a step count that differs from the nine-entry REFERENCE_SAMPLE throws under 'sample registration', and so does any title or caption mismatch that compareStep finds. That covers missing, extra or out-of-order steps, titles and captions. run() catches the failure, prints `FAIL [<phase>] ...` and sets exit code 1. In tests/e2e/verify-failures.test.ts, the faults 'sample removed from the registry' and 'sample titles out of order' check for a non-zero status, `FAIL [sample registration]`, and the slug or the offending step (step index 2, step 3 of 9). Judges A and C (pass) agree with this source. Judge B (fail) says the case where the steps content is absent reaches only a render timeout. That does not decide the requirement. STEPS is built from nine imports (steps/index.ts:1-25), and tsconfig.app.json sets noUnusedLocals: true. Emptying STEPS while those imports remain would therefore fail at the named 'build' phase. Reaching B's render-only path would require deleting the step files and rewriting the imports, which is a constructed deletion scenario the guidance says not to build. Removing some steps, reordering them, or unregistering the sample is caught explicitly by the sample-phase checks above.

audit_results.rationale: The quoted lines meet the requirement and the review guidance. If the reference presentation is not registered, checkRegistry() (scripts/verify.mjs:130-140) throws VerifyFailure('sample registration', ...). main() calls it right after the build and before any rendering (lines 373-377). run() catches the failure, prints `FAIL [<phase>] ...` through formatFailure, and returns exit code 1 (lines 413-429, 439). If the steps content is missing, extra or out of order, it is caught explicitly in the sample phase. A step count different from the nine-entry REFERENCE_SAMPLE throws 'sample registration' (lines 317-321). Any title or caption that is wrong or missing is reported by compareStep (lines 98-107) and thrown as 'sample registration' with the step label (lines 345-349). So these failures come from a check that reports the sample as missing or not matching the outline, not from an unrelated browser timeout. The tests back this up. In tests/e2e/verify-failures.test.ts, the faults 'sample removed from the registry' and 'sample titles out of order' assert a non-zero status, no PASS in the output, `FAIL [sample registration]`, and either the slug or 'step index 2 (step 3 of 9)' (lines 69-101 and 141-168). The dissent says that emptying the steps leads only to a render timeout. That depends on deleting step files or rewriting imports, which is a constructed partial-deletion scenario the guidance says not to build. The quoted steps/index.ts imports and tsconfig.app.json's noUnusedLocals also suggest that emptying STEPS while its imports remain would fail at the named build phase. Even if the hook read as 0, lines 310-316 would exit non-zero under a named phase ('render') rather than through a timeout. The guidance does not require a separate dedicated test because the check is explicit.

first_results.rationale: I'm ruling Judge A's and Judge B's pass verdict. None of the delivered test files drives a browser with a fixed sleep. Tests that involve a browser, tests/e2e/reference-verify.test.ts, tests/e2e/verify-failures.test.ts and tests/integration/inspect-presentation.test.ts, start the verify or inspect script with spawnSync, which blocks until the process exits. They then assert only on the exit status, output and manifest, so no assertion runs before the observed state exists. The only other async check, isPortOpen in tests/helpers.ts, is a direct TCP connect probe made after the process has exited, not a timed wait. The jsdom Presentation tests use Testing Library's waitFor, which polls. Judge C's reason does not decide the requirement, for two reasons. First, the delay(SETTLE_MS) it cites is in scripts/verify.mjs, the verification tool, not in a delivered test file. Second, that script does not use the delay in place of a state wait. Before the delay, waitForStepIndex polls with page.waitForFunction on data-step-index, and a missed step is still reported as a transition failure through the `arrived` result. The extra settle delay is the kind of fixed settle delay the guidance names as validator noise. So the step is never asserted after only a fixed sleep, and no test treats an immediately returning call as a wait.

results.rationale: Four delivered test files drive a real browser, all indirectly: tests/e2e/reference-verify.test.ts, tests/e2e/verify-failures.test.ts, tests/integration/inspect-presentation.test.ts and tests/integration/bootstrap-materialize.test.ts. Each starts `npm run verify` or the inspect helper with spawnSync, which blocks until that process has exited. Each then asserts only on the exit status, the output, the files written and the manifest. So no test asserts on browser state that is still changing, and none of the full test files quoted contains setTimeout, waitForTimeout, a sleep or a delay call. The only async helper they use, isPortOpen in tests/helpers.ts, is a direct TCP connection probe that resolves on connect or error. It runs after the child process has exited, and the test awaits it rather than treating it as a wait. The other UI test, Presentation.test.tsx, uses jsdom rather than a browser. It asserts synchronously after act()-wrapped key presses and fireEvent calls. Its one async check uses Testing Library's polling `waitFor`, and it has no timers. When the inspect helper used by the integration test reaches each step, it polls the step index with page.waitForFunction until data-step-index matches the target index. It then waits for a MutationObserver-based settle clock with a polling waitForFunction, not a fixed sleep. Judge A's pass and Judge B's pass match this material. Judge C's fail rests on `await delay(SETTLE_MS)` in scripts/verify.mjs:330. That line is in the verify script under test, not in the tests. It also follows a polling waitForStepIndex, so it is an extra settle delay after a state wait, not a sleep standing in for one. The criterion concerns how the browser tests wait before asserting. The tests assert only after the spawned process has exited, so C's reason does not decide the requirement.
